content: $\mathbb{T} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| = 1\}$. It is a compact metric space with the topology induced by $\mathbb{C}$. It is a multiplicative group with unit $e=1$ and $z^{-1} = \overline{z}$. It can be identified with the quotient group $\mathbb{R}/2\pi\mathbb{Z} = [-\pi, \pi)$.

$C(\mathbb{T}) = \{f: \mathbb{T} \to \mathbb{C} \text{ continuous}\} = \{f \in C([-\pi, \pi]) : f(\pi) = f(-\pi)\}$. The subspace $\Pi(\mathbb{T}) = \{f(t) = \sum_{k=-M}^{N} \alpha_k e^{ikt} : N, M \in \mathbb{N}, \alpha_k \in \mathbb{C}\}$ is the space of trigonometric polynomials.

concept: $C(\mathbb{T})$ as a Banach algebra and density of $\Pi(\mathbb{T})$
content: $C(\mathbb{T})$ is a Banach algebra with pointwise product and the norm $\|f\|_{\infty} = \sup_{t\in[-\pi,\pi]}|f(t)|$. The subspace $\Pi(\mathbb{T})$ is dense in $C(\mathbb{T})$.

1. $\sigma$-algebra definition. 2. $\sigma$-algebra generated by a family. 3. Borel $\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{B}(X)$. 4. For a Lebesgue measurable set $A \subset \mathbb{T}$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there exist compact $K$ and open $G$ with $K\subset A\subset G$ and $m(G\setminus K)<\varepsilon$. 5. Every Lebesgue measurable set $A$ is a Borel set union a null set. 6. Every Lebesgue measurable function equals a Borel measurable function almost everywhere.

A function $f: \mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C}$ is Lebesgue integrable if it is Lebesgue measurable and $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |f(t)|\, \frac{dt}{2\pi} < \infty$. The space $L^1(\mathbb{T})$ consists of equivalence classes $[f]$ of functions equal almost everywhere.
$L^1(\mathbb{T})$ is a Banach space with the norm $\|f\|_1 = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |f(t)|\, \frac{dt}{2\pi}$.
$C(\mathbb{T}) \subset L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and $\|f\|_1 \le \|f\|_{\infty}$ for $f\in C(\mathbb{T})$.

concept: Density of simple functions and continuous functions in $L^1(\mathbb{T})$
content: The spaces $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{T})$ (simple functions) and $C(\mathbb{T})$ are dense in $L^1(\mathbb{T})$.
$\Pi(\mathbb{T})$ is dense in $L^1(\mathbb{T})$.

A set function $\lambda: \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})\to[0,\infty]$ is a non‑negative measure if $\lambda(\emptyset)=0$ and $\lambda(\bigcup A_n)=\sum \lambda(A_n)$ for disjoint $A_n\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$. It is finite if $\lambda(\mathbb{T})<\infty$, $\sigma$‑finite if $\mathbb{T}=\bigcup A_n$ with $\lambda(A_n)<\infty$. It is regular if for every $A\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there exist compact $K$ and open $G$ with $K\subset A\subset G$ and $\lambda(G\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

(i) If $A_n\subset A_{n+1}$ then $\lim \lambda(A_n)=\lambda(\bigcup A_n)$. (ii) If $\lambda$ is finite and $A_{n+1}\subset A_n$ then $\lim \lambda(A_n)=\lambda(\bigcap A_n)$; the result fails without finiteness.

A set function $\mu: \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})\to\mathbb{C}$ is a complex measure if $\mu(\bigcup A_n)=\sum \mu(A_n)$ for disjoint $A_n$ (absolute convergence). The variation $|\mu|(A)=\sup\{\sum |\mu(A_n)| : A=\bigcup A_n, A_n\text{ disjoint}\}$. $\mu$ is regular if for every $A$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there exist compact $K$ and open $G$ with $K\subset A\subset G$ and $|\mu|(G\setminus K)<\varepsilon$.

Let $\mu$ be a complex measure. Then (i) $|\mu|$ is a non‑negative measure. (ii) It is the smallest non‑negative measure $\lambda$ satisfying $|\mu(E)|\le \lambda(E)$ for all $E\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$.
For any $z_1,\dots,z_n\in\mathbb{C}$ there exists a subset $S\subset\{1,\dots,n\}$ such that $\bigl|\sum_{j\in S}z_j\bigr| \ge \frac{1}{6}\sum_{j=1}^n|z_j|$.
If $\mu$ is a complex measure then $|\mu|$ is a finite measure.

Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and define $\mu(E)=\int_E f(t)\frac{dt}{2\pi}$ for $E\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$. Then (i) $\mu$ is a regular complex measure. (ii) $|\mu|(E)=\int_E |f(t)|\frac{dt}{2\pi}$. (iii) $\mu \ll m$ (absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure).

For non‑negative measures $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$, $\lambda_1\ll\lambda_2$ means $\lambda_2(E)=0\Rightarrow \lambda_1(E)=0$. For a complex measure $\mu$ and a non‑negative measure $\lambda$, $\mu\ll\lambda$ means $\lambda(E)=0\Rightarrow \mu(E)=0$.

Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2$ be finite non‑negative measures on $\mathbb{T}$. Then $\lambda_1\ll\lambda_2$ if and only if there exists $h\in L^1(\lambda_2)$, $h\ge 0$ a.e., such that $\lambda_1(E)=\int_E h\,d\lambda_2$ for all $E\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$.

Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\mathbb{T}$ and $\lambda$ a finite non‑negative measure. Then $\mu\ll\lambda$ (i.e. $|\mu|\ll\lambda$) if and only if there exists $f\in L^1(\lambda)$ such that $\mu(E)=\int_E f\,d\lambda$ for all $E\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$.

concept: Polar decomposition of a complex measure
content: Let $\mu$ be a complex measure on $\mathbb{T}$. There exists a measurable function $h$ with $|h(t)|=1$ for all $t$ such that $\mu(E)=\int_E h\,d|\mu|$ for all $E\in\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{T})$. We write $d\mu = h\,d|\mu|$.

$M(\mathbb{T})$ denotes the space of regular complex measures on $\mathbb{T}$ with norm $\|\mu\|_1 = |\mu|(\mathbb{T})$. $M_{ac}(\mathbb{T})$ is the subspace of measures absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure $m$.
(i) $L^1(\mathbb{T})$ is isometrically included in $M(\mathbb{T})$ via $f\mapsto \mu_f$, $\mu_f(E)=\int_E f\,dm$. (ii) $L^1(\mathbb{T}) = M_{ac}(\mathbb{T})$ with the same norm.

concept: Partition of unity for compact sets
content: Let $K$ be compact and $\Omega_1,\dots,\Omega_m$ open sets such that $K\subset\bigcup_{j=1}^m \Omega_j$. Then there exist $\varphi_j\in C(\mathbb{T})$ with $\operatorname{supp}\varphi_j\subset\Omega_j$, $0\le \varphi_j\le 1$, $\sum_{j=1}^m \varphi_j(x)\le 1$, and $\sum_{j=1}^m \varphi_j(x)=1$ for $x\in K$.
$M(\mathbb{T}) = (C(\mathbb{T}))^*$ with the same norm. That is, every bounded linear functional on $C(\mathbb{T})$ is given by integration against a unique regular complex measure.

For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(\mathbb{T})$ is the space of equivalence classes of Lebesgue measurable functions $f:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C}$ such that $\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} |f(t)|^p\frac{dt}{2\pi}<\infty$, with norm $\|f\|_p = \bigl(\int |f|^p\frac{dt}{2\pi}\bigr)^{1/p}$.
For a measurable $f:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C}$, the distribution function $\lambda_f$ is defined for $\lambda>0$ by $\lambda_f(\lambda) = m(\{t\in\mathbb{T}: |f(t)|>\lambda\})$.
If $f\in L^p(\mathbb{T})$ then (i) $\lambda_f(\lambda) \le \frac{1}{\lambda^p}\|f\|_p^p$. (ii) $\|f\|_p^p = \int_0^\infty p\lambda^{p-1}\lambda_f(\lambda)\,d\lambda$.

concept: A weak form of Hölder’s inequality
content: Let $1<p<\infty$ and $p'$ the conjugate exponent ($1/p+1/p'=1$). If $f\in L^p(\mathbb{T})$ and $g\in L^{p'}(\mathbb{T})$ then $fg\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and $\|fg\|_1 \le 2\|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'}$.
For functions $F,G$ on $\mathbb{T}^n$ the same method gives $\int |FG|\,dm_n \le 2\|F\|_p\|G\|_p$.
Let $1<p<\infty$ and $1/p+1/p'=1$. If $f\in L^p(\mathbb{T})$ and $g\in L^{p'}(\mathbb{T})$ then $\|fg\|_1 \le \|f\|_p\|g\|_{p'}$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, $(L^p(\mathbb{T}), \|\cdot\|_p)$ is a Banach space.
(i) $C(\mathbb{T})\subset L^p(\mathbb{T})$ and $\|f\|_p\le \|f\|_\infty$ for $f\in C(\mathbb{T})$. (ii) If $1\le p\le q<\infty$ then $L^q(\mathbb{T})\subset L^p(\mathbb{T})$ and $\|f\|_p\le \|f\|_q$.
For $1\le p<\infty$, the spaces $\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{T})$ (simple functions), $C(\mathbb{T})$, and $\Pi(\mathbb{T})$ (trigonometric polynomials) are dense in $L^p(\mathbb{T})$.

A measurable $f:\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{C}$ is essentially bounded if there exists $M\ge0$ such that $|f|\le M$ a.e. The essential supremum $\|f\|_\infty = \inf\{M : |f|\le M\text{ a.e.}\}$. $L^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ is the space of equivalence classes of essentially bounded functions.
For $f\in L^\infty(\mathbb{T})$: (i) $\|f\|_\infty = \inf_{m(N)=0}\{\sup_{t\notin N}|f(t)|\}$. (ii) There exists a null set $N_0$ such that $\|f\|_\infty = \sup_{t\notin N_0}|f(t)|$.
$(L^\infty(\mathbb{T}), \|\cdot\|_\infty)$ is a Banach space.

(i) $L^\infty(\mathbb{T}) \subseteq \bigcap_{p\ge1} L^p(\mathbb{T})$ and $\sup_{p\ge1}\|f\|_p \le \|f\|_\infty$. (ii) If $f\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and $g\in L^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ then $fg\in L^1(\mathbb{T})$ and $\|fg\|_1 \le \|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty$.
$C(\mathbb{T})$ is a closed subspace of $L^\infty(\mathbb{T})$ (identifying continuous functions with their equivalence classes).
